summary: The first word on the address: {the speaker} brings up {the point}: what the President said, and where they stand on it, from {their reason}. It can be one line, praise or scorn, and it doesn't have to end in a question. It doubles as the player's first look at the world: who this person is, what they do, what's going on in town.
realLife: One life: She sat in on morning coffee groups at gas stations and cafes, and in churches, where regulars, mostly retired or working men, plus a women's lunch group, talked politics as part of who they were and what they felt their places were owed. Another: Her study of barbershops and churches found political ideas form in everyday talk among neighbors and local figures, and most of it is about life, not about presidents and senators. Another: Most adults say politics comes up a little with family and friends, about one in five a lot. Families that agree talk more, and about two in five families avoid it. Another: Only about one in six adults feel comfortable talking politics with anyone, and people hold back most at work and around family. Another: A barber watched the inauguration on the shop TV and said he hoped the new President would deliver what he promised. A customer worried about who was and wasn't in the crowd. Another: Residents watched the address together at the diner. One said the talk of unity struck a chord; a server wanted to see action; a man in Montana was glad it mentioned God.
gates: {the speaker} holds {the address} on record, having watched it or heard of it from someone or the news.
{the speaker} has a stand on {the point}.
{the speaker} and the player are in the same place on record within a week of {the address}.
{the speaker} has not raised {the point} with the player before.
weights: How much {the point} touches {the speaker}'s life ({their reason}).
How engaged in politics {the speaker} is.
Whether the people present mostly agree: people bring politics up more among those who share their views, and hold back at work and with family when they don't.
The setting's habits: home and regulars' places more, work and strangers less.
choices: disagree, with the other side of the point
ask what it means for them

branches.when: {the speaker} is a local party officer or someone deep in politics
branches.then: They end on the party's next meeting or a rally, with the time and place on record, and the player can go.

branches.when: {the point} touches the player's own record (their job, their rent, their family)
branches.then: {the speaker} asks what the player thinks anyone should do about it, the first nudge toward doing something.

branches.when: {the speaker} and the player disagree and the setting is work
branches.then: {the speaker} drops it fast. The disagreement is recorded on the tie, and it colors the next talk.

branches.when: they watched {the address} together at home
branches.then: It can be one line, praise or scorn, with no question at the end. It's the intro, and it tells the player who this person is.
